body.explain: A fat-saturation pulse selectively excites and dephases the resonant frequency of fat protons before the imaging sequence, suppressing fat signal so it appears dark. This helps distinguish fat from enhancing tissue or hemorrhage that might otherwise be similarly bright.

body.prompt: This axial brain image is a diffusion-weighted scan (b-value 1000) obtained in a patient with acute onset neurologic symptoms. There is a focal area of markedly high signal. What does this finding most likely represent?
options: Acute ischemic stroke, where restricted diffusion from cytotoxic edema produces high DWI signal
A chronic old infarct, which typically shows high DWI signal as well
Normal brain parenchyma with no abnormality
A simple arachnoid cyst
body.explain: In acute ischemic stroke, cellular energy failure causes cytotoxic edema and restricted water diffusion, which produces markedly high signal on DWI within minutes to hours of onset, before changes are visible on conventional T1 or T2 sequences. Chronic infarcts typically show diffusion pseudonormalization or facilitated diffusion rather than restriction, and cysts follow free water signal, not restricted diffusion.

body.prompt: This axial brain image is a susceptibility-weighted scan showing a focal area of pronounced signal dropout (blooming). In the correct clinical context, what does this finding most likely represent?
options: Hemorrhage, since paramagnetic blood breakdown products cause local susceptibility artifact and signal loss
A simple fluid-filled cyst, which shows the same blooming pattern
Normal calcified choroid plexus with no clinical significance
A fat-containing lesion such as a lipoma
body.explain: Blood breakdown products such as deoxyhemoglobin and hemosiderin are paramagnetic and create local magnetic field distortion, producing pronounced signal loss on susceptibility-weighted imaging. This blooming effect is characteristic of hemorrhage and is used clinically to detect even small amounts of blood that other sequences may miss. Simple cysts and fat do not create this susceptibility effect.

body.prompt: This axial brain image is a post-contrast T1-weighted spin echo scan. There is a focal area of abnormal enhancement. What does contrast enhancement in a mass lesion typically indicate?
options: Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier or increased vascularity, allowing gadolinium to accumulate and shorten T1, as seen in many tumors
The lesion is definitely benign and requires no follow-up
The patient received an iodinated contrast agent that is directly visualized on MRI
Enhancement only occurs in old, chronic infarcts and never in tumors
body.explain: Gadolinium-based contrast agents shorten T1 relaxation time in tissue where they accumulate. Areas of blood-brain barrier breakdown or abnormal, leaky vascularity, common in many primary and metastatic brain tumors, allow gadolinium to accumulate and appear bright on post-contrast T1-weighted images. Enhancement pattern helps characterize a lesion but does not by itself prove it is benign, and MRI does not directly visualize iodinated CT contrast agents.

body.title: Contrast reactions: recognition and management
body.html:
Adverse reactions to a gadolinium-based contrast agent occur in roughly 0.07 to 2.4 percent of patients, and the vast majority are mild. True anaphylaxis is rare, on the order of 0.001 to 0.01 percent, and fatal reactions are rarer still. A transient feeling of warmth or flushing during injection is not a true reaction; reassurance is usually all it needs, and calming an anxious patient before the injection can prevent symptoms from escalating. Reactions are graded in three tiers. Mild reactions include nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, itching, and limited hives; the radiologist evaluates the patient, vitals are taken, and the patient is observed for up to 30 minutes. Moderate reactions such as diffuse erythema, bronchospasm, wheezing, hypotension, or a vasovagal episode are not immediately life threatening but can progress, so medical treatment and monitoring until resolution are required. Severe reactions include laryngeal edema, unresponsiveness, seizures, arrhythmia, and anaphylaxis, and demand immediate treatment.

Two low blood pressure pictures must be told apart. A vasovagal reaction, often triggered by anxiety around IV placement, produces hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, nausea, and sweating; the first maneuver is to elevate the legs or use Trendelenburg position to restore blood flow to the brain, then recheck vitals until the patient improves. Anaphylaxis produces hypotension with tachycardia, typically alongside hives, facial or laryngeal swelling, or wheezing, and it is the clear indication for epinephrine. A separate problem is extravasation, where contrast enters the soft tissue instead of the vein, causing swelling, redness, burning, and pain. A warm compress promotes reabsorption and circulation, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist should assess the site before the patient leaves.

When a reaction occurs, follow a rapid response sequence: remove the patient from the scanner and assess breathing, pulse, and consciousness; alert the covering radiologist and, if needed, the emergency response team; prepare the emergency equipment and medication box in a safe zone outside the magnetic field; inform responders of the study type, the agent given, and when the reaction began; then deliver medications exactly as the physician directs. The medication box pairs each drug with an indication: albuterol for wheezing, atropine for bradycardia, diphenhydramine for mild urticaria, dextrose for hypoglycemia, furosemide for pulmonary edema, and epinephrine for anaphylaxis. Per department protocol, the epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give decisively: 0.3 mg for patients 30 kg and over, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, pressed firmly against the lateral thigh until it clicks and held for several seconds. Every patient who receives an auto-injector goes to the emergency department for monitoring. Patients with a prior severe reaction are premedicated, commonly prednisone 50 mg by mouth 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before. Normal reference points while monitoring: SpO2 above 95 percent is normal and 92 percent or less suggests hypoxemia; normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and 80 diastolic.
keypoints: Reactions to gadolinium-based agents are uncommon and mostly mild; anaphylaxis occurs in roughly 0.001 to 0.01 percent of patients.
Vasovagal means hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, and sweating; anaphylaxis means hypotension with tachycardia plus hives or airway involvement.
For extravasation, a warm compress promotes reabsorption, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist assesses the site before discharge.
In an emergency: remove the patient from the scanner, alert the radiologist and response team, prepare equipment and the med box outside the field, inform responders, and deliver drugs as directed.

The epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give per department protocol: 0.3 mg at 30 kg and above, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, and every recipient goes to the emergency department.
body.worked_example: Five minutes after a gadolinium-based contrast injection, a patient develops spreading hives and begins to wheeze, with a heart rate of 118. Skin and airway involvement together meet anaphylaxis criteria, so this is treated as a severe reaction rather than a mild one. The technologist removes the patient from the scanner, checks breathing and pulse, alerts the covering radiologist, and moves the patient to a safe zone outside the magnetic field with the medication box and emergency equipment ready. Because both skin and airway are involved, the radiologist directs intramuscular epinephrine into the lateral thigh without delay, with albuterol as an adjunct for the wheeze, and the patient is monitored and sent to the emergency department.
memory_hooks: Slow and pale points vagal, fast with hives points anaphylaxis.
Compresses for extravasation: warm to clear it, cold to calm it.
The response flow spells RAPID: Remove, Alert, Prepare, Inform, Deliver.
exam_traps: Both vasovagal reactions and anaphylaxis drop the blood pressure; the heart rate separates them, slow for vasovagal and fast for anaphylaxis.
Warmth or flushing during injection is an expected sensation, not a true reaction, so the answer is reassurance rather than medication.
Diphenhydramine treats mild urticaria only; epinephrine, not an antihistamine, is the drug for anaphylaxis, and premedication reduces but does not eliminate repeat risk.

body.prompt: A patient develops scattered hives and itching a few minutes after a gadolinium-based contrast injection. Vital signs are normal. How is this reaction classified?
options: Mild, observe and notify the radiologist
Moderate, needing bronchodilator therapy
Severe, needing immediate epinephrine
Not a reaction, so no observation needed
body.explain: Urticaria with stable vitals is a mild reaction. The radiologist should still evaluate the patient, and observation for up to 30 minutes is appropriate because hives can progress.

body.prompt: During a contrast injection a patient develops stridor, facial swelling, and worsening difficulty breathing. Which severity category is this?
options: A mild reaction that resolves with reassurance
A moderate reaction managed with observation
A severe reaction requiring immediate treatment
A vasovagal episode managed with leg elevation
body.explain: Laryngeal edema signals a severe, potentially life threatening reaction. The emergency response sequence starts at once and epinephrine is prepared without delay.

body.prompt: Both a vasovagal reaction and anaphylaxis can drop the blood pressure. Which finding points to a vasovagal cause?
options: Bradycardia with pallor and sweating
Tachycardia with spreading urticaria
Wheezing with new facial swelling
Stridor with a rising heart rate
body.explain: Vasovagal reactions cause hypotension with a slow heart rate, pallor, and diaphoresis. Anaphylaxis typically pairs hypotension with tachycardia plus hives or airway symptoms.

body.prompt: A patient becomes pale, sweaty, and faint right after IV placement, with a slow pulse. What is the best first maneuver?
options: Elevate the legs to restore brain blood flow
Give an epinephrine auto-injector in the thigh
Apply a warm compress at the injection site
Administer an oral antihistamine right away
body.explain: This is a vasovagal reaction. Raising the legs or using Trendelenburg position returns blood to the brain while help is called and vitals are rechecked until the patient improves.

body.prompt: Contrast extravasates into the soft tissue of the forearm. What is the purpose of applying a warm compress?
options: It promotes reabsorption and circulation
It numbs the site and relieves the pain
It prevents infection at the puncture site
It constricts vessels to limit the swelling
body.explain: Warm compresses aid reabsorption of extravasated contrast by improving local circulation, while cold compresses are the choice for pain relief. A radiologist should assess the site before the patient leaves.

body.prompt: Which contrast reaction is the clearest indication for giving epinephrine?
options: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise
Nausea shortly after the injection
Isolated hives with stable vital signs
Warm flushed feeling during injection
body.explain: Epinephrine is the first line drug for anaphylaxis and severe bronchospasm. Nausea, isolated hives, or flushing do not call for it.

body.prompt: An anaphylactic reaction occurs in a child who weighs 20 kg. Which epinephrine auto-injector dose is correct?
options: 0.15 mg, the junior auto-injector dose
0.3 mg, the standard adult device dose
0.5 mg, repeated every three minutes
1 mg given slowly by intravenous push
body.explain: Children weighing 15 to 30 kg receive the 0.15 mg junior device. Patients at or above 30 kg, about 66 pounds, receive the 0.3 mg adult dose.

body.prompt: Per department protocol, which emergency drug may an MRI technologist administer on their own initiative during anaphylaxis?
options: Epinephrine by auto-injector
Diphenhydramine by IV push
Atropine from the med box
Nitroglycerin under the tongue
body.explain: The epinephrine auto-injector is typically the one medication a technologist may give decisively in an emergency. Every other drug in the box requires a physician to order and direct it.

body.prompt: After a technologist gives an epinephrine auto-injector for a contrast reaction, what must happen next?
options: The patient goes to the emergency department
The patient leaves once the hives have faded
The exam resumes when breathing feels normal
A second dose is always given ten minutes on
body.explain: Vital signs are watched closely and every patient who receives epinephrine goes to the emergency department, because symptoms can rebound and repeat dosing may be needed.

body.prompt: A patient with a prior severe reaction to gadolinium-based contrast is scheduled for a contrast MRI. What is a standard pre-medication schedule?
options: Prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7, and 1 hour before, plus diphenhydramine 1 hour before
Prednisone 50 mg as a single dose about 30 minutes before entering the scanner
Diphenhydramine 50 mg nightly for three days with no corticosteroid given at all
One epinephrine injection administered immediately before the contrast is dosed
body.explain: A common regimen is prednisone 50 mg by mouth 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast, with diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before. It lowers but does not eliminate the risk of a repeat reaction.

body.prompt: A patient begins wheezing after contrast administration. Which emergency medication box drug treats this symptom?
options: Albuterol, an inhaled bronchodilator
Atropine, which raises the heart rate
Furosemide, which clears excess fluid
Dextrose, which corrects low glucose
body.explain: Albuterol relieves bronchospasm and wheezing. Atropine treats bradycardia, furosemide treats pulmonary edema, and dextrose treats hypoglycemia.

body.prompt: During a contrast reaction the heart rate falls to 38 beats per minute. Which medication box drug addresses this finding?
options: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
Albuterol for airway smooth muscle
Aspirin for suspected cardiac ischemia
Nitroglycerin for severe anginal pain
body.explain: Atropine is the medication box drug for bradycardia. The physician directs its use; the technologist prepares the box but does not administer it.

body.prompt: The radiologist evaluates mild hives after contrast and requests treatment. Which drug matches this indication?
options: Oral diphenhydramine, an antihistamine
Intramuscular epinephrine at 0.3 mg dose
Nebulized albuterol to treat the rash
Sublingual nitroglycerin for comfort
body.explain: Mild urticaria is treated with 25 to 50 mg of oral diphenhydramine when the physician requests it. Epinephrine is reserved for severe reactions such as anaphylaxis.

body.prompt: While monitoring a patient after a contrast injection, which reading falls outside normal adult limits?
options: Oxygen saturation of 91 percent
Blood pressure of 118 over 76
Oxygen saturation of 97 percent
Resting pulse of 72 per minute
body.explain: An SpO2 above 95 percent is considered normal, and 92 percent or less suggests hypoxemia. Normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.

body.prompt: A patient reports feeling warm and flushed during the gadolinium-based contrast injection but has no other symptoms. What does this represent?
options: A common sensation, not a true reaction
An early mild reaction needing medication
The first stage of anaphylactic response
A vasovagal episode needing leg raising
body.explain: Transient warmth and flushing are expected sensations, not true reactions. Reassurance is usually all that is needed, and calming anxious patients before injection can prevent escalation.

body.title: Brain MRI: routine protocol and when to enhance
body.html:
A routine brain study uses the head coil and covers from the skull base to the vertex, roughly one slice above the top of the skull. Axial slices are angled along the AC-PC line, drawn through the anterior and posterior commissures, so that anatomy is displayed in a reproducible plane. Many departments now acquire 3D sagittal volumes (T1 or MPR, FLAIR, and T2) and reformat them into axial and coronal planes, which reduces repeat scanning and gives isotropic detail.

The non-contrast set is built around a signal triad. Diffusion detects acute infarct: true restriction is bright on the high b-value image (for example b1000) and dark on the ADC map. SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) shows hemorrhage and cerebral microbleeds in trauma and microhemorrhage. FLAIR is a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequence that nulls CSF so CSF appears dark, and it highlights multiple sclerosis and other white-matter disease. The spine equivalent for demyelination is STIR.

Gadolinium is dosed by body weight per department protocol. Structures that normally enhance confirm that contrast was delivered: the pituitary gland and infundibulum, choroid plexus, nasal mucosa and turbinates, dural venous sinuses, and vessels. Contrast is added by indication, such as routine with and without for headache or infection, tumor follow-up, pre-operative and immediate post-operative studies, metastatic or meningioma work-up in a patient with a cancer history, and demyelinating disease. Isolated memory loss usually does not receive contrast.
keypoints: Head coil, coverage skull base to vertex, axial slices angled on the AC-PC line.
Diffusion restriction means bright on high b-value AND dark on ADC.
SWI shows hemorrhage and microbleeds; FLAIR nulls CSF and shows MS.
3D sagittal volumes are reformatted into axial and coronal planes.
Gadolinium is weight-based; pituitary, choroid plexus, mucosa, sinuses, and vessels normally enhance.
body.worked_example: A patient arrives with sudden left-sided weakness. On the high b-value diffusion image a right frontal region is bright, and the same region is dark on the ADC map. That combination confirms an acute infarct with true restricted diffusion, so the finding is reported as acute stroke rather than dismissed as an artifact.
memory_hooks: Diffusion for stroke, SWI for blood, FLAIR for plaques.
True restriction is bright high-b, dark ADC.
AC to PC keeps every brain in the same plane.
exam_traps: FLAIR nulls CSF so CSF is dark, unlike T2 where CSF is bright.
High b-value brightness alone is not restriction without a dark ADC; bright high-b with bright ADC is T2 shine-through.

body.title: Specialized neuro studies: pituitary, IAC, and stereotactic planning
body.html:
The dynamic pituitary study uses the head coil and full-dose contrast. A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger. A dynamic contrast-enhanced sequence acquires rapid repeated images just after injection to catch microadenomas, which enhance later than the normal gland. On early dynamic frames the lesion therefore looks relatively dark against the briskly enhancing normal pituitary. Do not alter the dynamic sequence parameters. The gland has an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), the posterior lobe is often intrinsically T1-bright, and the gland sits in the sella turcica.

The internal auditory canal study also uses the head coil and full-dose contrast. The IAC carries cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear). Indications include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo or balance problems, tinnitus, and acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Technique combines thin-section heavily T2-weighted cisternal imaging, a steady-state CISS or FIESTA type sequence that outlines the nerves within bright CSF, plus thin post-contrast T1 with fat saturation. A related variant targets trigeminal neuralgia or facial-nerve problems such as facial pain or Bell's palsy involving CN VII.

Stereotactic or neuronavigation planning is a pre-surgical study. Keep the head straight and do not angle the slice packages, and acquire an isotropic 3D volume with full coverage. Do not clip the nose, ears, or back of the head, because the surgical navigation system registers the whole head surface. Sub-variants add perfusion for tumor grading or a dynamic sequence for metastases and meningioma, and a seizure pre-operative study angles coronals perpendicular to the hippocampus.
keypoints: Microadenoma is under 10 mm, macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger.
Dynamic pituitary catches microadenomas by their delayed enhancement, dark early against the normal gland.
IAC carries CN VII and VIII; indications include hearing loss and acoustic neuroma.
IAC uses thin-section CISS or FIESTA cisternal imaging plus post-contrast T1 fat-sat.
Stereotactic studies keep the head straight, do not angle packages, and never clip nose, ears, or occiput.
body.worked_example: A patient with a rising prolactin level has a normal-looking sella on routine images. The dynamic pituitary sequence is run, and on the earliest post-injection frames a small 6 mm region stays dark while the rest of the gland enhances briskly. That delayed enhancement pattern identifies a microadenoma that a single delayed image would have missed.
memory_hooks: Micro is under 10, macro is ten or more.
Seven and Eight run through the IAC gate.
Straight head, full head for navigation.
exam_traps: A microadenoma enhances later than the gland, so it looks dark early, not bright early.
Do not angle or crop the stereotactic packages; clipping the nose, ears, or occiput breaks surface registration.

body.prompt: Which coil and coverage are standard for a routine brain MRI?
options: Head coil, covering from the skull base to the vertex
Neck coil, covering from the orbits down to the carina
Body coil, covering from the vertex to the mandible only
Surface coil, covering the occiput and upper cervical spine
body.explain: Routine brain imaging uses a dedicated head coil and covers the skull base up to the vertex, about one slice above the top of the skull. The other coils and coverages do not include the whole brain.

body.prompt: Axial slices in a routine brain study are typically angled along which reference line?
options: The AC-PC line from the anterior to the posterior commissure
The orbitomeatal line from the outer canthus to the ear canal
The hard palate line drawn parallel to the maxillary teeth
The interhemispheric line drawn through the falx midline
body.explain: Axials are prescribed along the AC-PC line, drawn through the anterior and posterior commissures, giving a reproducible plane. The other lines are used for different purposes or planning steps.

body.prompt: On MRI, what confirms true acute restricted diffusion in a suspected stroke?
options: Bright signal on high b-value with dark signal on the ADC map
Bright signal on high b-value with bright signal on the ADC map
Dark signal on high b-value with dark signal on the ADC map
Dark signal on high b-value with bright signal on the ADC map
body.explain: True restriction is bright on the high b-value image and dark on the ADC map. Bright on both high-b and ADC is T2 shine-through, not restriction, and the dark-on-high-b patterns do not indicate acute infarct.

body.prompt: Which sequence is most sensitive for cerebral microbleeds and hemorrhage?
options: SWI, a susceptibility-weighted gradient technique
FLAIR, a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery technique
DWI, a diffusion-weighted echo-planar technique
STIR, a short tau inversion recovery fat-suppression technique
body.explain: SWI is highly sensitive to blood products and detects hemorrhage and microbleeds. FLAIR targets white-matter disease, DWI targets infarct, and STIR is used for fat-suppressed edema and cord imaging.

body.prompt: On a FLAIR image, how does normal CSF appear and what does FLAIR highlight?
options: CSF appears dark because it is nulled, highlighting MS plaques
CSF appears bright because it is enhanced, highlighting fresh blood
CSF appears gray because it is partly nulled, highlighting fat
CSF appears dark because it is saturated, highlighting cortical bone
body.explain: FLAIR nulls CSF so it appears dark, which makes periventricular MS plaques and white-matter disease stand out. FLAIR does not enhance CSF or specifically target blood, fat, or bone.

body.prompt: Many brain protocols acquire 3D sagittal volumes and then do what with them?
options: Reformat them into axial and coronal planes after acquisition
Discard them once the axial two-dimensional scans are complete
Send them only to the technologist workstation for archiving
Convert them into diffusion maps for stroke quantification only
body.explain: Isotropic 3D sagittal volumes such as T1, FLAIR, and T2 are reformatted into axial and coronal planes, giving multiplanar review from one acquisition. They are not discarded, merely archived, or turned into diffusion maps.

body.prompt: How is the gadolinium contrast dose for a brain MRI determined?
options: By the patient body weight, per the department protocol
By the patient age, using a fixed pediatric adult split
By the patient height, using a standard body surface chart
By a single fixed volume given to every patient equally
body.explain: Gadolinium is dosed on body weight following department protocol. It is not set by age, height, or a single fixed volume for all patients.

body.prompt: Which structure normally enhances and can confirm that gadolinium was given?
options: The pituitary gland and infundibulum, which enhance normally
The cerebral cortex, which enhances briskly in every patient
The normal white matter tracts, which enhance after injection
The lateral ventricle CSF, which enhances soon after injection
body.explain: The pituitary and infundibulum lack a blood-brain barrier and enhance normally, along with choroid plexus, nasal mucosa, dural sinuses, and vessels. Normal cortex, white matter, and CSF do not enhance.

body.prompt: Which clinical situation typically does NOT warrant contrast on a brain MRI?
options: Isolated memory loss without other concerning history
Follow-up of a known brain tumor after prior treatment
Work-up for metastatic disease in a known cancer patient
Immediate post-operative imaging after a tumor resection
body.explain: Isolated memory loss is usually imaged without contrast. Tumor follow-up, metastatic work-up, and immediate post-operative studies all routinely use gadolinium.

body.prompt: What size threshold separates a pituitary microadenoma from a macroadenoma?
options: 10 mm, with micro under 10 and macro 10 or larger
20 mm, with micro under 20 and macro 20 or larger
5 mm, with micro under 5 and macro 5 or larger
15 mm, with micro under 15 and macro 15 or larger
body.explain: A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger. The 20, 5, and 15 mm figures are not the accepted threshold.

body.prompt: On an early dynamic pituitary frame, how does a microadenoma usually appear?
options: Relatively dark, because it enhances later than the normal gland
Brightly enhancing, because it fills with contrast before the gland
Isointense, because it enhances exactly with the normal gland
Completely absent, because it never takes up any contrast agent
body.explain: A microadenoma shows delayed enhancement, so on early dynamic frames it looks relatively dark against the briskly enhancing normal gland. It does not enhance first, match the gland, or fail to enhance entirely.

body.prompt: Which statement about the normal pituitary gland is correct?
options: The posterior lobe is often T1-bright and the gland sits in the sella turcica
The anterior lobe is always T1-dark and the gland sits in the cavernous sinus
The posterior lobe is always T2-bright and the gland sits above the clivus
The anterior lobe is often T1-bright and the gland sits in the frontal sinus
body.explain: The posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) is frequently intrinsically T1-bright, and the gland lies within the sella turcica. The other pairings misplace the gland or misassign the bright signal.

body.prompt: Which cranial nerves run through the internal auditory canal?
options: The facial nerve VII and the vestibulocochlear nerve VIII
The trigeminal nerve V and the abducens nerve VI together
The glossopharyngeal nerve IX and the vagus nerve X together
The optic nerve II and the oculomotor nerve III together
body.explain: The IAC carries CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear). The other pairs travel through different skull base routes, not the internal auditory canal.

body.prompt: Which finding is a classic indication for an internal auditory canal study?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss with suspected acoustic neuroma
Sudden thunderclap headache with suspected aneurysm rupture
Progressive memory loss with suspected early dementia change
New focal seizures with suspected cortical developmental lesion
body.explain: The IAC protocol targets sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Aneurysm, dementia, and seizure work-ups use other protocols.

body.prompt: Which technique best displays the CN VII and VIII within the IAC?
options: Thin-section heavily T2-weighted CISS or FIESTA steady-state imaging
Thick-slab T1-weighted spin echo imaging without any fat saturation
Standard axial gradient echo imaging matched to the routine brain
Low-resolution single-shot diffusion imaging through the posterior fossa
body.explain: Thin-section heavily T2-weighted steady-state imaging (CISS or FIESTA) outlines the nerves against bright CSF, and thin post-contrast T1 fat-sat is added. Thick T1, routine gradient echo, and diffusion do not resolve the nerves.

body.prompt: When planning a stereotactic neuronavigation study, how should slices be prescribed?
options: Keep the head straight and do not angle the slice packages at all
Angle the axial package along the AC-PC line as in routine brain
Angle the coronal package perpendicular to the hippocampal body
Tilt the whole package toward the side of the suspected lesion
body.explain: Navigation studies require the head straight with unangled packages so the volume registers cleanly to the surgical system. AC-PC angling and hippocampal angling belong to other protocols, and lesion tilting is not done.

body.prompt: Why must a stereotactic planning volume include the entire head surface?
options: The navigation system registers the whole head surface for guidance
The radiologist needs the neck vessels included for perfusion mapping
The scanner requires full coverage to correct for gradient nonlinearity
The surgeon uses the sinuses alone to align the operative approach
body.explain: The surgical navigation system registers the full head surface, so the nose, ears, and occiput must not be clipped. The other reasons do not drive the full-coverage rule for planning volumes.

body.prompt: The trigeminal-neuralgia and facial-nerve variant of the IAC study targets which nerve?
options: The facial nerve CN VII in patients with facial pain or Bell's palsy
The optic nerve CN II in patients with sudden painless vision loss
The hypoglossal nerve CN XII in patients with tongue deviation signs
The accessory nerve CN XI in patients with shoulder droop weakness
body.explain: The variant evaluates CN VII for facial pain or Bell's palsy, alongside trigeminal assessment. The optic, hypoglossal, and accessory nerves are not the focus of this protocol.

body.title: Spine MRI protocols: cervical, thoracic, and lumbar
body.html:
The cervical spine is imaged with a combined head and neck coil for indications such as neck pain, herniated disc (HNP), degenerative disc disease (DDD), radiculopathy, stenosis, cord compression, MS, tumor, Chiari malformation, syrinx, and radiating arm pain. Sagittal coverage runs from the pons and fourth ventricle down to about T2 to T3, pedicle to pedicle, and axials extend from C2 to C3 through C7 to T1, angled to each disc space. Core sequences are Sag T2 and Sag T1 for herniation, DDD, lesions, tumor, and syrinx, plus Sag STIR for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection. Axial GRE displays the nerve roots and osteophytes, and Ax T2 shows cord lesions and syrinx. An anterior saturation band placed in front of the vertebral bodies suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion and also reduces CSF pulsation artifact.

The thoracic spine covers roughly C7 to L1 for mid back pain and the same degenerative and cord indications. Because the thoracic levels are hard to count, a vitamin E capsule (a common skin or table marker) is placed to help count vertebral bodies so the correct level is localized. Sag STIR is the best sequence for MS, infection, fracture, and bony metastases. Add Cor T2 for scoliosis and Cor STIR when neurofibromatosis (NF1 or NF2) is suspected. Axials may use right to left phase encoding to push breathing motion artifact away from the cord.

The lumbar spine covers about T12 to S2 with axials from L1 to S1 for low back pain, HNP, DDD, radiculopathy, stenosis, tumor, radiating leg pain, prior surgery, and tethered cord. Use an odd number of slices per disc (for example 5) so one slice runs through the disc center. Contrast is required for infection, post-operative scarring, and tumor. After back surgery, contrast separates enhancing scar (fibrosis) from non-enhancing recurrent disc. Tethered cord studies extend coverage down to the coccyx.
keypoints: Cervical uses a head and neck coil; sagittals run from the pons and fourth ventricle to about T2 to T3.
Sag STIR is best for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection in every region of the spine.
Axial GRE shows nerve roots and osteophytes but blooms near metal, so avoid it there.
An anterior saturation band suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion plus CSF pulsation.
A vitamin E capsule marker counts thoracic levels; lumbar covers about T12 to S2 with odd slices per disc.
body.worked_example: A patient returns with recurrent leg pain one year after an L4 to L5 discectomy. A plain non-contrast study cannot tell whether the epidural soft tissue is scar or a new disc fragment. Contrast is given, and the tissue enhances uniformly, which identifies fibrosis rather than recurrent disc. Because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not, the post-operative lumbar spine is protocoled with contrast from the start.
memory_hooks: STIR lights up the bad marrow: MS, mets, fracture, infection.
Vitamin E dot lets you count the vertebral bodies and find the level.
Post-op scar glows, recurrent disc stays dark.
exam_traps: Do not run GRE near spinal hardware, because metal blooms and hides the anatomy.
The post-operative lumbar spine gets contrast because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not.

body.title: Total spine and technique: bone versus neuro, drop metastases, and metal reduction
body.html:
A total spine is assembled from two sagittal packages, an upper and a lower set, that overlap by about two disc spaces at 3 mm with no gap. The upper package uses a smaller field of view than the lower one. Always use the smallest field of view that still covers the anatomy, and adjust resolution whenever the FOV changes. Remember the counts: the spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae. Routing depends on the order. A cervical, thoracic, and lumbar BONE order is run as three separate studies, while a NEURO order is run as a single total spine.

Metastatic disease splits into two patterns. Drop metastases seed down the CSF from a primary brain tumor, so the study images the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum and typically omits the pre-contrast axials. Bony metastases arise from primary cancers such as lung, colon, or breast, usually need no contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence can help characterize marrow. Cor STIR is added when neurofibromatosis is suspected. For post-contrast technique, use a fat-saturated T1 to improve differentiation of enhancing tissue, and do not simply append a pre-contrast inversion recovery T1 as the post series.

Near hardware, a metal reduction toolkit recovers the image. Use TSE (turbo spin echo) rather than gradient echo, increase the receive bandwidth, and raise the turbo or echo train factor. Decrease the slice thickness, switch fat-saturated T2 to STIR for more uniform fat suppression, and decrease the TE. Raise the resolution, change the phase encode direction, and increase the number of signal averages to recover lost signal.
keypoints: A C, T, and L BONE order runs as three separate studies; a NEURO order runs as one total spine.
Total spine sagittals use two packages overlapping by about two disc spaces at 3 mm with no gap.
Drop mets seed from a brain tumor and require imaging the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum.
Bony mets from lung, colon, or breast usually need no contrast; in and out of phase can help.
Near metal, use TSE not gradient echo, raise bandwidth, and switch fat-sat T2 to STIR.
body.worked_example: A patient with a known posterior fossa primary is sent for spine imaging to look for CSF seeding. Because drop metastases fall through the CSF and collect at the bottom of the thecal sac, the coverage is extended to include the entire sacrum, and the pre-contrast axials are omitted so the post-contrast series does the work. A patient with lung cancer and back pain, by contrast, is worked up for bony metastases, usually without contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence helps confirm marrow replacement.
memory_hooks: Bone order splits into three, neuro order joins into one.
Drop mets fall to the floor, so scan all the way to the sacrum.
Fight metal with TSE, wide bandwidth, and STIR.
exam_traps: A C, T, and L BONE order is run as separate studies, while a NEURO order is run as one total spine.
Near metal, prefer STIR over fat-saturated T2 and use TSE rather than gradient echo.

body.prompt: Which coil is standard for imaging the cervical spine?
options: A combined head and neck coil covering the cervical region
A dedicated extremity coil wrapped around the lower neck
A single small loop surface coil taped over the throat
The transmit body coil alone with no surface coil added
body.explain: The cervical spine is imaged with a head and neck coil, which places receive elements over the whole cervical region for adequate signal and coverage.

body.prompt: On a cervical spine study, how far superiorly should the sagittal coverage extend?
options: To the pons and fourth ventricle, then down to about T2 to T3
To the vertex of the skull, then down to the mid lumbar spine
To the hard palate only, then down to the level of the carina
To the frontal sinus region, then down to the top of the sacrum
body.explain: Cervical sagittals cover from the pons and fourth ventricle down to about T2 to T3, pedicle to pedicle, so the cervicomedullary junction and cervicothoracic junction are included.

body.prompt: Which sagittal sequence is best for showing MS plaques, metastases, fracture, and infection?
options: Sagittal STIR, which brightens cord edema and marrow lesions
Sagittal T1 gradient echo tuned with a very long echo time
Axial gradient echo optimized only to display the nerve roots
A low resolution localizer acquired with wide slice gaps only
body.explain: STIR suppresses fat and makes edema conspicuous, so it is the best sequence for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection where marrow or cord signal is abnormal.

body.prompt: Axial GRE shows nerve roots and osteophytes well, but should be avoided when what is present?
options: Metallic hardware, because susceptibility causes signal blooming
A simple midline disc bulge without any associated bony change
Cerebrospinal fluid pulsation moving along the cervical cord
Mild degenerative scoliosis of the lower thoracic spinal column
body.explain: Gradient echo is very sensitive to susceptibility, so metal blooms and obscures the anatomy. Near hardware a TSE based sequence is used instead.

body.prompt: An anterior saturation band placed in front of the vertebral bodies primarily reduces what?
options: Swallowing, breathing, and cardiac motion, plus CSF pulsation
Chemical shift misregistration at the fat and water boundaries
Magnetic susceptibility blooming caused by dental restorations
Gibbs truncation ringing seen at sharp high contrast interfaces
body.explain: A saturation band in front of the spine nulls signal from the moving throat, heart, and chest, which suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion and also reduces CSF pulsation artifact.

body.prompt: On a thoracic spine study, why is a vitamin E capsule marker placed on the patient?
options: To count vertebral bodies so the correct level is localized
To suppress fat signal along the anterior chest wall region
To trigger the acquisition to the patient breathing cycle
To calibrate the transmit gain before the scan is started
body.explain: The thoracic levels are hard to count, so a bright vitamin E marker gives a fixed reference on the images that lets the reader count vertebral bodies and localize the correct level.

body.prompt: What is the usual sagittal coverage range for a lumbar spine study?
options: About T12 down to S2, covering the conus and the thecal sac
About C7 down to L1, covering the mid spinal column segments
About L3 down to the coccyx, a narrow and focused lower block
About the pons down to L1, matching a cervical spine package
body.explain: Lumbar sagittals span about T12 to S2 so the conus medullaris and the lower thecal sac are both included, with axials typically from L1 to S1.

body.prompt: Why does the post-operative lumbar spine require contrast?
options: Scar tissue enhances while recurrent disc material does not
Contrast shortens the total scan time for the whole examination
Contrast removes all of the motion artifact from axial images
Recurrent disc enhances brightly while scar tissue stays dark
body.explain: After back surgery, enhancing fibrosis and non-enhancing recurrent disc look similar without contrast. Because scar enhances and recurrent disc does not, contrast separates the two.

body.prompt: A herniated disc or a syrinx is best demonstrated on which weighting?
options: T2, where bright fluid makes a syrinx and disc herniation stand out
T1 without contrast, where fluid appears uniformly dark instead
Gradient echo alone, which is reserved mainly for metallic clips
A proton density map optimized purely for marrow fat contrast
body.explain: T2 makes fluid bright, so a syrinx and a herniated disc against dark structures stand out clearly, which is why Sag and Ax T2 are core to spine protocols.

body.prompt: How should a cervical, thoracic, and lumbar BONE order be performed?
options: As three separate studies, one for each region of the spine
As a single total spine using one continuous sagittal package
As a limited single sagittal localizer of the whole spinal axis
As a combined brain and whole spine screening survey protocol
body.explain: A BONE order for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar is run as three separate studies, whereas a NEURO order is run as one total spine.

body.prompt: How are the sagittal packages of a total spine study assembled?
options: Two packages that overlap by about two disc spaces, no gap
Two packages that abut with a wide gap between the two sets
Two packages that overlap by about half the entire spinal column
One single package for the whole spine, so overlap never applies

Use the largest FOV available to capture nearby structures
Match the FOV to the bore size regardless of the anatomy
Keep the FOV fixed at 40 cm for every spine examination

Image only the cervical cord where the seeding begins first
Stop coverage at L1 since the cord ends around that level
Cover the brain alone because the sacrum stays unaffected

A double dose of contrast with delayed post-contrast imaging
Intrathecal contrast injected before the sagittal series runs
Oral contrast timed to the start of the axial image acquisition

Decrease the receive bandwidth to widen each frequency voxel
Lower the echo train factor toward a single spin echo readout
Increase the slice thickness to average the artifact together
body.explain: A higher receive bandwidth shortens the readout and reduces the spatial spread of susceptibility, which cuts metal artifact. Raising the echo train factor and thinner slices also help.

body.prompt: Near metallic hardware, fat-saturated T2 should be switched to what?

A spectral fat-sat T1 acquired with a very short echo time
Gradient echo, which handles the susceptibility more cleanly
A plain T2 with no fat control and a very long echo time set
body.explain: Spectral fat saturation fails near metal because the field is distorted. STIR uses an inversion time to null fat and gives more uniform suppression around hardware.

body.prompt: Which sequence family is preferred over gradient echo near hardware?

GRE, because its single pulse shortens the readout echo time
Echo planar imaging, because it fills k space very rapidly
Balanced steady state, because it maximizes the fluid signal
body.explain: TSE (turbo spin echo) applies refocusing pulses that recover signal lost to susceptibility, so it is preferred over gradient echo near metal.
